parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what makes the thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale different from the Celsius scale - where does it choose to place its zero point?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Absolute Zero Means**
Think of temperature as a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles. There is a lowest possible limit where particles have minimum energy. That limit is absolute zero.

Step 2: **The Kelvin Starting Point**
The thermodynamic scale is defined so that it starts exactly at that limit. So absolute zero is $$T = 0\text{ K}$$ with the unit kelvin, symbol $\text{K}$, written without a degree sign.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a liquid-in-glass thermometer actually measures - is it temperature itself, or the expansion of one particular liquid?
parts.proper_answer: The measured temperature depends on the properties of the thermometric liquid used, whereas thermodynamic temperature does not depend on the properties of any substance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What You Really Measure**
A liquid-in-glass thermometer does not measure temperature directly. You see the length of the liquid column, which depends on how much that particular liquid expands.

Step 2: **Why That Is Not Thermodynamic**
Different liquids expand by different amounts and in different non-linear ways. So two thermometers with different liquids would give slightly different readings between fixed points. True thermodynamic temperature is defined to be independent of the properties of any one material.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the shape and direction of the graph in Fig. 2.2 - what happens to $\rho$ as $T$ increases, and is the change steady or curved?
Hint 2: For a good thermometer you need to be able to convert one measured value back to one and only one temperature easily - how does this graph help with that?
parts.proper_answer: Resistivity varies with temperature, giving a unique value of resistivity for each temperature. The variation is linear, allowing simple calibration.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A Property That Changes**
Fig. 2.2 shows $\rho$ increases as $T$ increases. That is essential - if resistivity did not change, measuring resistance would tell you nothing about temperature.

Step 2: **Linear and Unique**
The graph is a straight line. That means $$\rho \propto T \text{ (linear)}$$ over the range shown. A straight line also means each value of $T$ gives one unique value of $\rho$, and vice versa. So you can calibrate easily and read temperature directly from resistance with equal sensitivity at all temperatures.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 2.1 - think about the size of the glass tube and platinum assembly and what must happen thermally before it reads correctly.
parts.proper_answer: The thermometer has a large heat capacity so takes a long time to reach thermal equilibrium with the surroundings.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Big Object Needs More Heating**
Look at Fig. 2.1. There is a large glass tube, a plastic strip and a coil of wire. All of that material must warm up or cool down to the temperature you want to measure.

Step 2: **Slow to Follow Fast Changes**
Because its heat capacity is large, a lot of energy transfer is needed for a change in temperature. If the environment temperature is changing rapidly, the thermometer lags behind and never reaches equilibrium in time.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about which thermometer type uses a tiny junction of two wires with very small mass and almost no thermal inertia.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Need Small and Fast**
For rapidly changing temperature you need something with very low heat capacity that reaches equilibrium almost instantly.

Step 2: **Best Choice**
A thermocouple uses a small junction of two different metals. Its mass is tiny, so it follows temperature changes very quickly and is ideal here.

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what NTC means for how resistance behaves when temperature rises, and compare that direction and shape to the straight rising line for platinum in Fig. 2.2.
parts.proper_answer: For an NTC thermistor resistance decreases as temperature increases (inverse variation) and the variation is non-linear, unlike the linear increase for platinum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Opposite Direction**
NTC means negative temperature coefficient. As $T$ goes up, resistance goes down. Platinum does the opposite - its resistivity and resistance go up with $T$.

Step 2: **Different Shape**
Platinum gives a straight-line graph in Fig. 2.2. A thermistor gives a curved, non-linear fall in resistance with temperature, much more sensitive over a small range but harder to calibrate linearly.
